questions.title: Detecting spare receptors
questions.question: Which of the following statements about spare receptors is most correct?

options.A: Spare receptors activate the effector machinery of the cell without the need for a drug
options.B: Spare receptors, in the absence of drug, are sequestered in the cytoplasm
options.C: Spare receptors may be detected by the finding that the EC50 is greater than the Kd for the agonist
options.D: Spare receptors will be detected if the intracellular effect of drug-receptor interaction lasts longer than the drug-receptor interaction itself

explanations.A: Incorrect. Spare receptors still require a drug to bind and trigger the effector machinery; they are simply the extra receptors left unoccupied once enough others have already driven the response to its maximum, not receptors that self-activate without any drug at all.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Spare receptors are ordinary surface receptors, present and available for binding at all times, not receptors hidden away in the cytoplasm in the absence of drug.
explanations.C: Incorrect. This reverses the true relationship: the presence of spare receptors is detected when a tissue's EC50 is lower, not greater, than the agonist's Kd for the receptor -- the tissue reaches half-maximal effect before the receptor is half-occupied.
explanations.D: Correct. Spare receptors exist when a tissue's maximal response is reached with less than full receptor occupancy. One reliable way this is detected experimentally is that the intracellular effect of the drug-receptor interaction outlasts the binding interaction itself -- the signal set in motion by transient receptor occupancy continues after the drug has already dissociated, which is only possible when enough receptors and downstream amplification exist that full occupancy was never required for the maximal signal.

questions.topic: Receptor Regulation and Variation in Drug Responsiveness
questions.learning_objective: Recognise that spare receptors are detected when a drug's intracellular effect outlasts the drug-receptor interaction itself.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Spare receptors will be detected if the intracellular effect of drug-receptor interaction lasts longer than the drug-receptor interaction itself"

questions.title: When receptor up-regulation occurs
questions.question: Regarding receptor up regulation, one of the following statements is true:

options.A: It may involve decrease in the effectiveness of receptors.
options.B: It usually occurs after chronic administration of an agonist.
options.C: It usually involves a decrease in the number of receptors
options.D: It occurs after chronic administration of an antagonist.

explanations.A: Incorrect. A decrease in receptor effectiveness describes down-regulation/desensitisation, not up-regulation, which instead produces hyperactivity or supersensitivity.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Chronic agonist administration produces receptor down-regulation (desensitisation), not up-regulation -- this option reverses the true agonist/antagonist relationship.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Up-regulation involves an increase, not a decrease, in the number of receptors, since prolonged antagonist contact drives synthesis of new receptors.
explanations.D: Correct. Receptor up-regulation follows long-term exposure of cells to an antagonist, which frequently produces hyperactivity or supersensitivity of the receptors: prolonged antagonist contact drives synthesis of new receptors, so the tissue ends up with more receptors than baseline. This is why abruptly stopping a chronically-taken antagonist -- a beta-blocker, for example -- can precipitate worsening angina or dysrhythmias, since the enlarged receptor population is suddenly exposed to endogenous agonist with nothing left to block it.

questions.topic: Receptor Regulation and Variation in Drug Responsiveness
questions.learning_objective: State that receptor up-regulation occurs after chronic administration of an antagonist, not an agonist.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: It occurs after chronic administration of an antagonist."

questions.title: Definition of tachyphylaxis
questions.question: Tachyphylaxis refers to which of the following?

options.A: Responsiveness decreased rapidly after administration of a drug
options.B: Responsiveness increased rapidly after maintenance of a drug (hypersensitive)
options.C: Responsiveness increased rapidly after administration of a drug
options.D: Responsiveness decreased rapidly after maintenance of a drug (desensitized)

explanations.A: Correct. Tachyphylaxis is a decrease in the intensity of response to a drug that develops rapidly -- after the first dose or only a few doses -- rather than gradually over a longer course. This is what separates it from ordinary tolerance, which is the same kind of falling response but developing slowly with sustained use.
explanations.B: Incorrect. "Increased" responsiveness is the wrong direction for tachyphylaxis, which is specifically a decrease, and "after maintenance" describes a gradual rather than a rapid timescale.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Tachyphylaxis is a decrease, not an increase, in responsiveness; increased responsiveness after a drug would instead describe hyperreactivity or sensitisation, not tachyphylaxis.
explanations.D: Incorrect. "After maintenance" describes a gradual process (ordinary tolerance or desensitisation over a longer course), whereas tachyphylaxis is specifically defined by its rapid onset, after the first or first few doses.

questions.learning_objective: Define tachyphylaxis as a rapid decrease in drug response after administration, distinct from gradual tolerance.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Responsiveness decreased rapidly after administration of a drug"

questions.title: Term for increased intensity of drug response
questions.question: Which of the following refers to an increased intensity of response to a drug?

explanations.A: Correct. Hyperreactive describes quantitative variation in drug response -- an individual showing an increased intensity of response to a standard dose, more than most people would show. This is a dose-response phenomenon, distinct from a genetic (idiosyncratic) or immunological (hypersensitive) cause of an unusual reaction.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Idiosyncratic describes a qualitatively different response caused by a genetic difference in drug metabolism or receptor structure, not simply an increased intensity of the expected response.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Hypersensitive specifically names an allergic or immunological drug response, a different mechanism from a purely quantitative increase in the expected pharmacological effect.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Tolerance is a decrease, not an increase, in response with repeated dosing -- the opposite direction from what this question asks about.

questions.learning_objective: Identify hyperreactive as the term for an increased intensity of quantitative response to a drug, distinct from idiosyncratic and hypersensitive.

questions.title: Rapid loss of calcitonin's effect in hypercalcaemia
questions.question: A 44-year-old black male is brought to the emergency department with 6 h of worsening lethargy and confusion. Past medical history is significant for easy bruising, 3 months of bone pain, and frequent pneumococcal infections. Labs were ordered, revealing serum calcium of 17 mg/dL (normal: 9.0 to 10.5 mg/dL). To rapidly lower his serum calcium, you administer calcitonin. However, calcitonin alone is insufficient because it is known to rapidly and suddenly lose its effectiveness within 2 to 3 days of repeated dosing, for which reason a bisphosphonate, which takes 2 to 3 days to become effective, is added simultaneously. What is the term for the rapid decrease in response to calcitonin?

explanations.A: Correct. Calcitonin's effectiveness fading within 2-3 days of repeated dosing is the textbook example of tachyphylaxis: a decrease in response that appears rapidly, after only the first few doses, rather than gradually over a long course. This is exactly why a bisphosphonate -- slower to start but not subject to the same rapid fade -- is begun at the same time, so it takes over calcium control once calcitonin's effect has tachyphylaxed away.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Ordinary tolerance is also a fall in response with repeated dosing, but it develops gradually over a longer course; the stem specifically describes a rapid loss within days, which is the defining feature of tachyphylaxis rather than tolerance.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Anaphylaxis is a severe, acute systemic allergic reaction, an unrelated concept to a drug's effectiveness fading with repeated dosing.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Prophylaxis means preventive treatment altogether, not a description of a drug's response fading with repeated administration.

questions.learning_objective: Apply the tachyphylaxis definition to the clinical vignette of calcitonin's rapidly-fading effect in severe hypercalcaemia.

questions.title: Transporter for renal excretion of drugs
questions.question: The transporter protein which responsible for the excretion of some drugs into the urine is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. MDR1 (P-glycoprotein) is a well-known efflux transporter, but it is not the specific transporter this teaching point names for urinary drug excretion.
explanations.B: Incorrect. ABC (ATP-binding cassette) is the broad superfamily that MRP itself belongs to, not the specific named transporter for renal drug excretion this question asks for.
explanations.C: Incorrect. SLC (solute carrier) transporters are instead named for the uptake of some neurotransmitters, the opposite direction and a different substrate from renal drug excretion.
explanations.D: Correct. MRP (multidrug resistance-associated protein) is the transporter protein responsible for excreting some drugs into the urine at the renal tubule. It is a specific, named efflux transporter, distinct from the general carrier-mediated transport mechanism taught alongside it. Renal elimination overall combines glomerular filtration, active tubular secretion (where transporters like MRP act) and passive tubular reabsorption, and MRP-mediated secretion is one concrete, named example of that active step.

questions.learning_objective: Name MRP as the transporter protein responsible for excreting some drugs into the urine.

questions.title: Transporter for neurotransmitter uptake
questions.question: The transporter protein which responsible for the uptake of some neurotransmitters is:

explanations.A: Correct. SLC (solute carrier) transporters are responsible for the cellular uptake of some neurotransmitters, such as at a presynaptic nerve terminal. This is a specific, named uptake transporter, distinct in both substrate and direction from MRP, which instead excretes drugs into urine. Terminating a neurotransmitter's action by reuptake through an SLC transporter is also the mechanism several drug classes exploit or block therapeutically.
explanations.B: Incorrect. MRP (multidrug resistance-associated protein) is instead named for excreting some drugs into the urine at the renal tubule, the opposite direction (efflux, not uptake) from the neurotransmitter uptake this question asks about.
explanations.C: Incorrect. ABC (ATP-binding cassette) is the broad transporter superfamily that MRP belongs to, not the specific named transporter for neurotransmitter uptake.
explanations.D: Incorrect. MDR1 (P-glycoprotein) is a well-known efflux transporter, not the transporter named for neurotransmitter uptake.

questions.learning_objective: Name SLC as the transporter protein responsible for the cellular uptake of some neurotransmitters.

questions.title: How water-soluble drugs are absorbed
questions.question: Water soluble drugs are absorbed mainly by:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Active transport needs a specific carrier protein and energy, and is reserved for particular drugs resembling endogenous substrates, not the general route for water-soluble drugs.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Pinocytosis engulfs fluid and large or particulate substances by membrane invagination (iron being the worked example), not the typical route for ordinary small water-soluble drug molecules.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Passive diffusion through the lipid membrane favours small, lipid-soluble, non-ionised molecules -- the opposite of a water-soluble drug, which cannot readily dissolve through the lipid bilayer.
explanations.D: Correct. Filtration moves small, water-soluble drugs through aqueous membrane pores or paracellular channels, carried along with bulk water flow rather than dissolving through the lipid membrane. This is exactly the route suited to a water-soluble, rather than a lipid-soluble, molecule, which cannot readily dissolve through the lipid bilayer that passive diffusion depends on. It requires no carrier protein and no energy, unlike active transport.

questions.learning_objective: State that water-soluble drugs are absorbed mainly by filtration through aqueous membrane pores.

questions.title: How iron is absorbed
questions.question: Iron is absorbed mainly by:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Filtration through aqueous pores is reserved for small water-soluble molecules, not the worked mechanism taught for iron's absorption.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Active transport requires a specific carrier and energy against a gradient; it is not the mechanism this teaching point names for iron.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Passive diffusion favours small, lipid-soluble, non-ionised molecules crossing directly through the lipid membrane, not the route taught for iron.
explanations.D: Correct. Pinocytosis engulfs fluid together with dissolved or particulate substances by membrane invagination, forming a vesicle that carries the material into the cell. Iron is the worked pharmacokinetic example of a substance absorbed mainly by this route. This mechanism is distinct from the diffusion, filtration and carrier-mediated mechanisms taught alongside it, since it does not require the substance to cross the membrane at all -- the membrane instead wraps around it.

questions.learning_objective: State that iron is absorbed mainly by pinocytosis.
